extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, science/health journalists, press officers, and medical communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing presence and consequences of 'spin' (misleading emphasis of benefit) in press releases and related news coverage of randomized controlled trials, and factors associated with such misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "spin"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Spin," defined as specific reporting strategies (intentional or unintentional) emphasizing the beneficial effect of the experimental treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operational definition used to identify problematic wording/strategies in abstracts, press releases, and news items; examples are shown in the paper's figures (e.g., Figure 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of spin in scientific article abstract conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of 'spin' in the abstract conclusion of the scientific article (observed in 28/70, 40%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a potential source of downstream misrepresentation; in multivariable analysis, the presence of spin in the article abstract conclusion was strongly associated with spin in the press release (RR 5.6, 95% CI 2.8–11.1, p < 0.001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of spin in press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the press release contains 'spin' (identified in 33/70, 47%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by applying the study's 'spin' definition to press release text; presence of spin in press releases was associated with prior spin in article abstracts and led to overestimation of trial findings in a substantial fraction of cases (see overestimation metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of spin in news items / media coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether related news items report the trial with 'spin' (21/41 news items, 51%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many news items reproduced the same type of spin as the press release and article abstract; assessment compares news wording to source materials to identify spin propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overestimation of RCT findings based on press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether findings of RCTs, when interpreted from the press release alone, are overestimated (observed for 19/70 reports, 27%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized by comparing the interpretation obtainable from the press release to the actual results reported in the scientific article (i.e., press-release-derived conclusions that exaggerate benefit relative to the article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overestimation of RCT findings based on news items
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether findings of RCTs, when interpreted from the news item alone, are overestimated (observed for 10/41 news-item reports, 24%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed by comparing news-item claims to the trial's reported results; often linked to replication of spin from press releases or abstracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency/propagation of spin across abstract, press release, and news
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the type of 'spin' appearing in the abstract conclusion is the same as that in the press release and in related news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found that news items were mainly reported with the same type of spin as identified in the press release and article abstract conclusion, implying propagation of specific misleading strategies downstream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate factors associated with spin in press releases (variables assessed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables considered for association with presence of spin in press releases: journal type, funding source, sample size, type of treatment (drug or other), results of the primary outcomes (all nonstatistically significant versus other), author of the press release, and presence of spin in the abstract conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these variables, only presence of spin in the article abstract conclusion was independently associated with spin in the press release (multivariable RR 5.6). This implies evaluators should examine abstracts as a primary predictor of press-release quality.
